newsitem.title: CROATIA: Albright to press Croatia, Serbia on peace accords.
newsitem.headline: Albright to press Croatia, Serbia on peace accords.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright is due to meet Croatian and Serbian leaders on Saturday to demand their full compliance with the 1995 Dayton peace accords for Bosnia.

Albright, who arrived in Zagreb late on Friday, was making her first trip to the Balkans to drive home the point that the United States and other Western powers were determined to ensure the U.S.-brokered Bosnian peace deal did not completely unravel.
"There is no alternative to Dayton -- except for the horrors that Dayton ended," Albright said earlier in Sintra, Portugal, at an international meeting on Bosnia.
The United States and its allies, fearing Bosnia's peace process was in danger of unravelling, ordered the former warring factions to comply with the Dayton peace accords or else face sanctions.
In their toughest ultimatum since the accords were signed 18 months ago, they threatened a series of punitive measures, including action against anyone "harbouring" Bosnia's indicted war criminals.

The United States, Britain and France, the main contributors to a NATO-led force in Bosnia, fear that unless the peace accords are implemented in full, the Balkan country could slip back into war after foreign troops leave as scheduled in June 1998.
Croatian President Franjo Tudjman and Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic were key signatories to the Dayton accords and must be held to their commitments, U.S. officials said.

Albright would "lay out in crystal clear terms what the bar is (that both governments must meet) and what the consequences are if they don't," a senior U.S. official told reporters on the Secretary of State's flight from Portugal to Croatia.

One U.S. official said the new U.S. envoy to Bosnia, Robert Gelbard, received some suggestions during a trip to Croatia and Serbia this week that Tudjman and Milosevic would work with Albright but "it would be a mistake to expect concrete results" during her visit.

Albright would press Tudjman to comply with a Dayton pledge to bring war criminals to justice before The Hague tribunal and would seek an end to the harassment of Serb refugees trying to to return to Croatia's Eastern Slavonia and Krajina regions, U.S. officials said.

They said she was expected to warn that Washington might support a delay in the return of Eastern Slavonia from U.N. administration to Croatian control if Zagreb did not improve treatment of Serbs, said the officials.

Albright would also warn that U.S. support for international loans to Croatia and for Croatia's entrance into Western institutions like NATO's "Partnership for Peace" programme depended on adherence to the Dayton peace deal and other international standards.
The officials said Albright would fly by helicopter to the Krajina region to visit a burned out house and to meet a refugee family.
The aim was to stress the importance of Zagreb preventing harassment of Serbs and allowing their return to the region after being driven out during the Balkan conflict.
Albright was due to fly to Belgrade later in the day to press Milosevic to cooperate in delivering war criminals to the Hague tribunal.
She would ask Milosevic to get his Bosnian Serb allies to live up to their Dayton obligations.
Albright would also urge Milosevic to permit greater political autonomy in Serbia's Kosovo region, which is largely populated by ethnic Albanians, and to move towards democracy in his country.
U.S. officials say there has been a worsening trend in Serbia on political and press liberties.

If Milosevic could show concrete results in these areas the United States was prepared to "engage him step by step" in a process that would lift the "outer wall of sanctions" imposed by Washington, the officials said.
These included U.S. opposition to international financing for Serbia, Serbian membership of the United Nations and other organisations, and full-scale diplomatic relations.
During her trip to Belgrade, Albright will visit the Czech embassy where she lived as a child when her father was ambassador to Yugoslavia.
Born in Czechoslovakia, she emigrated to the United States to escape communism.
